title: Mario, Kirby & Nintendo Platforming
blurb: Launch-week Nintendo remasters give way to original handheld platforming, with a couple of non-Nintendo mascots crashing the party.
games: A launch-window remake of Super Mario Bros. 2 (the US version) with Mario Bros. classic mode bundled in, built to show off what the GBA screen could do.
Super Mario Advance 2: Super Mario World
The SNES classic in your pocket, largely unchanged and none the worse for it.
A faithful port of the SNES original's painterly art style, still one of the best-looking 2D platformers Nintendo ever made.
Super Mario Advance 4: Super Mario Bros. 3
Adds e-Reader card support and a redrawn HUD to the NES classic many still call the best 2D Mario game.
A pyramid full of theme-park-ride levels and a ticking escape-the-dungeon finale, widely considered the series' high point.
A remake of the original NES Kirby's Adventure with copy abilities intact, brighter and friendlier than the 8-bit original.
Splits Kirby into four and opens up a genuinely non-linear map, the series' first real detour into Metroidvania territory.
A puzzle-platformer spiritual sequel to the Game Boy's Donkey Kong '94, guiding Mini Marios through hazard-filled toy factories.
Sega's answer to the question of whether 2D Sonic could survive on a handheld, co-developed with Dimps after Sonic Team's own attempts stalled.
A 2D reimagining of the PS1 platformer's dream-logic world, swapping out the original's pseudo-3D visuals for flat sprite work.

title: Action-Adventure & Metroidvania
blurb: This is the console generation that turned “Metroidvania” from a joke term into a genre — four different franchises prove it here.
games: A tighter, more linear Metroid built around the parasitic X organism and a persistent SA-X stalker that turns exploration into horror.
A full remake of the original NES Metroid with a stealth-driven post-game epilogue that reframes Samus's origin story.
A GBA launch title that leans harder into RPG-style card-fusion systems than any Castlevania before it.
Two overlapping castles and a soundtrack that split fans down the middle, from the same team that would go on to make Aria of Sorrow.
Widely considered the best of the GBA Castlevania trilogy, built around a soul-collecting system that replaced sub-weapons with real build variety.
The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past & Four Swords
The SNES classic plus a brand-new four-player-only multiplayer dungeon crawl, playable only over link cable.
The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap
A shrinking-and-growing gimmick built into a fully original Zelda, developed by the same Capcom studio behind Oracle of Ages and Seasons.
Boktai: The Sun Is in Your Hand
Hideo Kojima's vampire-hunting action-RPG ships with a literal solar sensor in the cartridge that reads real sunlight to power your weapon.
A darker, harder reboot of the Mega Man X formula with rank-based mission scoring, kicking off a beloved four-game series.

A Pokémon developer side project starring a girl and her drill-powered vehicle, built entirely around momentum and rotation puzzles. Never released in Europe on the original cartridge — European players had to wait until a 2016 Wii U Virtual Console release.

title: Role-Playing Adventures
blurb: Camelot's original Golden Sun duology anchors a chapter stacked with Square Enix remasters and a run of Japan-only tactical RPGs that took years to reach the West, if they ever did.
games: An original GBA RPG built around elemental Djinn and environmental puzzle-solving, one of the console's true system-sellers.
A direct continuation told from the villains' point of view, expanding the first game's Psynergy puzzle mechanics considerably.
A standalone tactical RPG set in a world literally rewritten by children's imagination, distinct from the PS1 Final Fantasy Tactics.
A remake of the SNES classic with an added post-game dungeon and rebalanced difficulty, developed under Square Enix's supervision.
Brings the job-system-heavy SNES original West with new jobs and a bonus dungeon, years after fans had only known it through fan translations.
The trilogy's closer adds new espers and a bonus dungeon to what many consider the strongest 16-bit Final Fantasy.
Tactics Ogre: The Knight of Lodis
A prequel to the SNES tactical RPG classic, notable as developer Quest's final release before its assets were absorbed into Square. Released in Japan and North America, but never in Europe.
A menu-driven, item-focused RPG that strips out overworld exploration entirely in favor of tightly scripted story chapters. Released in Japan and North America, but never in Europe.
An action-RPG about forging your own weapon from summoned spirits, taking three years to reach North America after its Japanese release — and never reaching Europe at all.

A direct sequel with a dual-protagonist structure, released in North America the same year as its predecessor despite years separating their Japanese launches — like the first game, it never reached Europe.
A compressed retelling of the Lunar: Silver Star Story saga, trading the PS1 original's anime cutscenes for a much smaller handheld canvas.

title: Pokémon & Monster-Collecting
blurb: A smaller chapter than its GB and GBC predecessors, but no less foundational — this is the generation that introduced double battles and abilities.
games: The third generation's home base, introducing double battles, Abilities, and a new region built around weather manipulation.
The definitive version of the Hoenn generation, adding the Battle Frontier's toughest post-game gauntlet yet.
Remakes of the original Red and Blue rebuilt on the Ruby/Sapphire engine, with the Sevii Islands added as new post-game content.
Pokémon Mystery Dungeon: Red Rescue Team
A roguelike dungeon-crawler spin-off where you play as a Pokémon yourself, built on Chunsoft's own long-running Mystery Dungeon engine.
A sequel to the Game Boy Color pinball spin-off, rebuilt around the Hoenn region's new roster.

title: Strategy & Tactics
blurb: Advance Wars turned Nintendo's own long-running Japan-only Wars series into a global hit; Fire Emblem's Western debut wasn't far behind.
games: A colorful reboot of the Japan-only Famicom Wars series that became an unexpected worldwide hit, its Japanese release delayed for years over the game's military theme.
A direct sequel adding new commanding officers and a harder campaign, released well before Japan finally got either game.
The series' first game ever localized outside Japan, bundling in a tutorial-friendly prologue built specifically to teach newcomers permadeath tactics.
A stand-alone, branching-path sequel that lets you freely grind and explore the world map, unusual for the series.

A card-driven tactical RPG about rallying a defeated princess's army, built around a unique union-based battle formation system. Europe only got a limited release, through 505 Games in select countries like Italy and France.
An obscure turn-based squad tactics game from X-COM creator Julian Gollop, reviving a series that started on 1980s home computers.
A card-battle RPG following the anime's Duelist Kingdom and Battle City arcs, deep enough to work as a real strategy game on its own terms.

title: Fighting
blurb: Full console-caliber fighting games compressed onto a cartridge, from Guilty Gear's frame-perfect combos to a licensed Dragon Ball Z brawler built for the format.
games: A shockingly faithful port of Arc System Works' own arcade fighter, frame data and all.
A handheld conversion of Capcom's arcade fighter with the full Isms system and roster intact.
A 2D reimagining of the console game's 3D fighting engine, built to keep fatalities and the series' brutal tone on original hardware.
A surprisingly deep fighter starring Sonic's whole cast, with a lengthy single-player story mode wrapped around the versus battles.
A 2D arena fighter spanning the Saiyan through Cell arcs, co-developed by the same studio behind Guilty Gear.
The King of Fighters EX2: Howling Blood
A 3D-modeled-sprite fighter adapting SNK's team-battle series for a handheld screen.
The first Tekken game ever on a Nintendo platform, reworked from 3D into a 2D fighter to fit the hardware.

title: Shooters & Run-and-Gun
blurb: Treasure's name appears three times in this chapter alone — the GBA quietly became one of the best shoot-em-up platforms of its generation.
games: A from-scratch handheld Metal Slug with new stages, keeping the series' chaotic run-and-gun spectacle intact at a smaller resolution.
Contra Advance: The Alien Wars EX
A remake of the Super NES's Contra III built by the studio that would later make Hotel Dusk, not a straight console port.
A spiritual sequel to the Genesis cult classic Gunstar Heroes, packing the same absurd boss-rush density into a handheld cartridge.
A licensed beat-em-up/shooter hybrid guided by Astro Boy creator Osamu Tezuka's own manga continuity, widely considered one of Treasure's best.
A Mode-7-style rail shooter pushing pseudo-3D scaling effects further than most developers thought the GBA's hardware allowed.
A surprisingly complete port of id Software's FPS classic, built by a small studio rather than id itself.
A side-scrolling reimagining of the one-liner-spouting mercenary's world, trading first-person shooting for run-and-gun platforming.
A genre hybrid pairing a full top-down shoot-em-up with an RPG leveling and dialogue layer wrapped around it.
A beat-em-up adaptation of the Sega Saturn cult classic, trading some of the original's chaos for tighter handheld pacing.

title: Sports & Racing
blurb: Camelot's handheld-companion sports duo returns, joined by original GBA racers and a surprisingly faithful Tony Hawk's port.
games: Bundles every Super Mario Kart SNES track in as unlockable content alongside a full new roster of its own, one of the GBA's best-selling games.
A launch-window F-Zero built around pure high-speed racing with no weapons, from a then-new Nintendo-affiliated studio.
A companion to the GameCube's Mario Golf with its own RPG-lite training campaign rather than a stripped-down port.
Deepens the training-academy structure from Mario Golf: Advance Tour into a genuinely long single-player RPG-tennis hybrid.
An isometric-3D handheld build of the skating classic, developed entirely separately from the GBC sidescroller that preceded it.
An overhead arcade racer with a surprisingly deep track editor for a game few people noticed at release.
A kart racer starring Konami's own mascot cast, built as a launch-window answer to Mario Kart.
An arcade off-road racer co-developed with a Polish studio, remembered mainly by GBA completionists.

title: Puzzle & Party
blurb: WarioWare's microgame format was practically invented for a handheld — this chapter is anchored by its two best entries.
games: Dozens of five-second microgames strung into one absurd package, a format so novel it spawned its own sub-genre.
Ships with a gyro sensor built into the cartridge, controlled entirely by physically tilting the system.
A one-button rotating-stick maze game, deceptively simple and never officially released in North America.

Dig straight down through color-coded blocks without getting crushed, ported to GBA years after its arcade and Dreamcast debut. Europe actually got it over a year earlier than North America, in early 2004.
An offbeat tile-matching puzzler starring a sentient pair of trousers, one of Rare's odder post-Nintendo-era handheld games.
A block-clearing puzzler from the small Scottish studio it's named after, praised for a difficulty curve that never feels unfair.
A word-spelling puzzle game that turned a browser casual-game hit into a legitimate handheld pack-in favorite.
Trades the series' board-game format for a microgame-and-minigame collection built specifically around handheld play sessions.
An RPG-structured single-player Bomberman adventure, built around exploring an island and collecting battle-mode power-ups.

title: Adventure, Action & Licensed
blurb: Proof that licensed and ported games on GBA weren't automatically shovelware — several of these are genuinely well-regarded conversions.
games: A grapple-hook-driven action game that plays like a handheld cousin to Bionic Commando, released in Europe as Ninja Cop.
Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars
A point-and-click adventure classic self-ported by its original developer, streamlined for a D-pad and two buttons.
A puzzle-platforming spin-off built around boss rush challenges, arriving in North America three years after its Japanese release.
A top-down reimagining of the noir shooter's bullet-time gunplay, built from scratch for the handheld rather than a straight port.
A beat-em-up tied to the 2003 animated reboot, developed in-house by Konami rather than outsourced.
A top-down reimagining of the original 1997 Grand Theft Auto's free-roaming crime sandbox, built to run natively on GBA hardware.
An original handheld Crash platformer rather than a console port, well-regarded enough to be remembered fondly outside the mainline series.
A launch-window original Spyro platformer built specifically for GBA, not a downgrade of any PS1 game.
A boxing game tied to the film franchise with its own distinct handheld-built gameplay, separate from the PS2/Xbox version's engine.
Bruce Lee: Return of the Legend
A side-scrolling martial-arts action game loosely inspired by Bruce Lee's films, built by the same studio behind Crash's handheld outings.

title: Simulation & Strategy-Sim
blurb: A small chapter, but a varied one — a beloved farming sim sits alongside a chess engine, a mecha strategy spin-off, and a genuine 1986 relic.
games: Harvest Moon: Friends of Mineral Town
A gender-flippable remake of the SNES-era farming sim's Mineral Town setting, still considered one of the series' most replayable entries.
A full-featured chess engine and tutorial system squeezed onto a handheld cartridge, tournament-strength AI included.
A turn-based RPG about customizing an armed car and battling your way across a post-apocalyptic desert.
Zone of the Enders: The Fist of Mars
A side-story spin-off of Konami and Hideo Kojima's mecha-action series, built as a top-down action-RPG rather than a 3D shooter.
A handheld port of the 1986 Cinemaware medieval-strategy classic, one of the oldest games in this whole collection by original release date.

title: Cult Classics & Japan-Only Curios
blurb: The deepest cuts in the collection — including two games, Mother 3 and Rhythm Tengoku, that remain among the most requested Nintendo localizations that never happened.
games: A remake of the original Game Boy Seiken Densetsu, rebuilt with full RPG-scale sprites and split dual-protagonist storylines.
A Japan-only rhythm-game anthology that would go on to spawn the Rhythm Heaven series once it finally reached the West on DS.
The long-awaited EarthBound sequel, released only in Japan after its English localization was cancelled — later revived by a celebrated fan translation.
Widely considered the peak of the action-RPG spin-off series that reimagined Mega Man as a hacker battling viruses across a stylized internet.
The first game in a whole Japan-only platforming series starring a starfish prince, never localized until a much later DS sequel.
A Metroidvania built by a small Canadian studio, notable for context-sensitive gadgets that let you replay earlier areas differently.
A loose remake of Rare's own 1984 ZX Spectrum classic, reworked into a top-down jungle-maze adventure.

A pinball spin-off of Sega's House of the Dead light-gun series, zombies and all, built by the developer behind Sega's Pinball series. Unusually, it launched in North America a few weeks before Japan, with Europe following about a year later in 2003.
A movie tie-in shooter that ended up considerably more competent than the notoriously panned film it was based on.
